What brokers or stream-processing frameworks that market 'exactly-once' are typically actually providing is at-least-once delivery under the hood, combined with deduplication logic -- built into the broker's client, a specific integration (like exactly-once support scoped to writes within the same system, e.g. Kafka-to-Kafka), or a transaction/idempotency mechanism -- that makes duplicates invisible for the specific, supported code paths it covers. The moment a consumer's processing involves a side effect the broker doesn't natively manage as part of that exactly-once mechanism -- calling a third-party payment API, sending an email through an external provider, writing to a completely different downstream system -- that side effect is exposed to the underlying at-least-once reality: a redelivered message (from an ack that timed out, a consumer crash-and-restart, or a rebalance) will trigger that external side effect again unless the consumer itself checks whether it's already handled that specific message. So the practical takeaway is to treat 'exactly-once' claims as scoped to whatever the broker/framework specifically covers, and build idempotency directly into any consumer logic with an externally-visible side effect -- typically by recording a processed message ID durably, ideally atomically with the side effect itself -- rather than trusting the delivery layer alone to make duplicates someone else's problem.

assessments.prompt: A service inserts a new order into its own database, then, as a separate subsequent step, calls the broker to publish an OrderPlaced event. The process is killed by the orchestrator between those two steps. Per the concept's discussion of the dual-write problem, what is the standard mitigation?
options: Increase the process's retry count for the publish call so it eventually succeeds no matter what.

Write the event into an outbox table as part of the SAME database transaction as the order itself, so both commit together or neither does, and have a separate relay process read the outbox and publish to the broker afterward.
Switch from at-least-once to at-most-once delivery, so the broker never redelivers a message.
Have the broker poll the service's database directly instead of receiving explicit publish calls.
assessments.explanation: The concept names this exact mitigation: "the transactional outbox pattern... the service writes the event into an 'outbox' table in the SAME database transaction as the actual state change, guaranteeing both succeed or both fail together; a separate relay process then reads the outbox and publishes to the broker." Option A doesn't address the actual gap -- if the process was already killed before the publish call ran at all, retrying a call that never happened doesn't help. Option C is unrelated and would make message loss more likely, not solve the atomicity gap between the two writes. Option D fabricates a broker capability (directly polling an arbitrary service's database) that isn't part of any pattern described in the concept.

assessments.prompt: Per the concept, in what two specific senses is a producer in an event-driven architecture decoupled from its consumers, beyond simply 'not calling them synchronously'?
options: Decoupled in geography and in currency, since producers and consumers are usually billed separately.

Decoupled in time (a consumer doesn't need to be running or even deployed yet when the event is produced) and in knowledge (the producer's code contains no reference to who consumes its events or what they do with them).
Decoupled in programming language and in database vendor.
Decoupled in security permissions and in encryption algorithm.
assessments.explanation: The concept states this precisely: the producer "is decoupled from its consumers in time (a consumer doesn't need to be running, healthy, or even deployed yet at the moment the event is produced...) and in knowledge (the producer's code contains no reference to who consumes its events, how many consumers exist, or what they do with them)." The other options invent decoupling dimensions -- geography/currency, language/database vendor, security/encryption -- that are never discussed in the concept as defining properties of event-driven decoupling.

assessments.prompt: Per the concept's explanation of delivery guarantees, why do most practical systems build 'effectively-once' behavior on top of at-least-once delivery rather than relying on a broker's literal exactly-once guarantee?
options: Because at-least-once delivery is always faster than exactly-once delivery under every possible network condition.

Because guaranteeing literal exactly-once delivery to a remote, independently-failing process across an unreliable network is not something any real distributed system can honestly promise end-to-end, so systems instead combine at-least-once delivery with consumer-side idempotency to achieve the same practical outcome.
Because exactly-once delivery is only supported by brokers that don't support ordering guarantees.
Because at-most-once delivery is a legal requirement for financial transactions, making at-least-once the only remaining option.
assessments.explanation: The concept states this directly: "delivering a message to a remote, independently-failing process exactly one time, guaranteed, across an unreliable network and possible crashes on either end, is not something any real distributed system can honestly promise end-to-end -- what most systems that advertise 'exactly-once' are actually providing is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing." Option A makes an unsupported performance claim not discussed anywhere in the concept. Option C fabricates a nonexistent relationship between ordering support and exactly-once delivery. Option D invents a legal-requirement claim not present in the material, and additionally misidentifies which guarantee is described as the practical default (at-least-once, not at-most-once).
